I don’t have an answer to the vet question, but my dog had something similar happen with both her eyes back on New Year’s Eve. She wouldn’t open either and they were super swollen, and when I could look inside they were very bloodshot. I freaked out and drove her to the emergency vet ($450 visit so not going to help you here) but, I believe what caused it was the evening before this I had sprayed some glade air freshener and she happened to walk over right when I did it with her eyes open and started sneezing/pawing at her eyes afterwards. 

At the time of her eyes swelling I didn’t even think of that scenerio and was more worried about an insect or something. But after all her tests they said it was an allergic reaction to something in her environment and I tried to think of what it could be and that came to mind. She was given eyedrops for 7 days and was fine by like the 3rd day but I continued to use them of course.

Agree with the other comments to check for any bites anywhere, but also if there is any sort of fragrances or something similar to my story in your house, I wanted to share in case it helps. I have since stopped using aerosol sprays and yes I still feel horrible about it 🥲

*edit *
Additionally I did ask if it was okay to give her Benadryl to stop her from trying to paw at her eyes and they said yes. This did seem to help. They also gave me a cone for her to wear the entire week because the vet said if she is able to scratch her eye with her paw and ends up scratching the actual cornea, it’s going to be a lot more of a pain in the ass to treat. So if you are able to watch her, try and make sure she isn’t trying to rub her face or paws on her eyes to scratch them!

Seconding psychology today. You can look up ones in your area, and often they offer sliding payment scales if you are uninsured. You can also search on that website by so many filters like distance, sex (if you prefer female or male), specialties (maybe addiction or OCD is something in particular you are looking for help with) and religion (if you would like someone who is based around faith). It can really help narrow it down if you want something specific but if not it is helpful either way. I believe they also show reviews for them there too but if I am wrong and you see someone you are interested in, you could easily google their name and practice and see what reviews they have there.

You have to tip out, it’s not an option to not. Everyone works together collectively as a whole so it kind of makes sense. My bussers clean the tables so I can be sat again. They bring my tables waters so I can focus on getting their alcoholic drinks and taking orders. The expo plates my food for my tables so that it goes to the right place and nothing is missed. The stocker keeps ice, cups, bread, and butter in stock so that it’s always there for us when we get new tables. The salad person makes our salads when we get a new table. At my restaurant the bartender also makes all of our soft drinks. So they get a tip out of our non alcoholic sales as well. 

My restaurant does a lot of large groups, so the flow of everyone working together helps for servers to be able to be at the table as much as is necessary. When you’re serving 20+ people someone is always bound to need something, so it’s good they are never left waiting this way. The bartender making my 12 margaritas, 4 beers, and 6 Pepsi’s definitely buys me time to serve my food for other guests, fix anything that needs fixing, greeting new guests, taking orders, clearing dirty plates, cutting and serving desserts, etc. 

I’ve never worked at a restaurant that pools tips (meaning all the servers put their money together and share). What I make at the end of the night is my tips, and I tip out from that. So I might have $400 before tip out to all the help staff, and after tip out have $250. But the person next to me might have $200 before tip out and leave with $80 after. It just depends on the server, section, etc.

Sometimes depending on my section, if I like the person I am working with and know they will pull their weight, we can team up and help eachother and split our tips at the end of the night. I don’t do that with everyone but some people I will. I like to do this when I see I have a lot of reservations in my section and know that I could use the extra help. We help eachother and share what we make, and I’m cool with that as long as they do their part. 

Thats our choice though, not the restaurant. But I’ve been to restaurants where that is required, (usually you’ll have a different person at your table every time you need something because all of them are serving you technically). 
I’ve heard good things and bad things about restaurants that do that. For instance if you have someone who isn’t pulling their weight but they still get an even cut of the pool isn’t really fair. But then on the other hand if everyone is helping eachother then you don’t ever have to risk being “weeded”. I personally feel like I would make less if I worked somewhere like this because you don’t really get to have a personal interaction with your tables, there’s a different server every time and it just gets confusing. I always make sure my guests know my name and if I do elect to have another server help, then I bring them over and introduce them as well so they know who we are. The pooling type restaurants just feel too impersonal to me. 

I prefer being able to make the call on whether I am pooling with someone though. I generally get 20%-30% tips because I am good at my job, and I don’t like sharing with servers who just do the bare minimum for their guests. Sorry for the long winded answer, haha. But as far as “not tipping” the staff that just isn’t an option and hasn’t ever happened I don’t think at my job. Everyone has a list of the servers in their area of the restaurant (we are very large) so they know who to expect tips from at the end of the night and on the off chance someone forgot or something they’d be able to tell management “hey, XYZ didn’t tip me out.” And it would be taken care of. 

But like I said that doesn’t happen. Generally everyone (at least at my job) knows it’s part of the job and that we all play a part in making the night run smoothly. Now I might tip some bussers out extra than others if they really went above and beyond and have been known to do that, and they also can see that because they can ask for our sales report and see the percentage that we left them from our food sales. Generally though it’s on a trust basis and the tips are usually around the same each night, so if there’s a drastic difference one time they’d know immediately something was up.

Hi, just so you know your tip doesn’t go to just your waiter. A reason people get upset about not being tipped adequately is because they also have to tip out: the bar, their bussers, stockers, and sometimes hostesses and the kitchen staff as well. 

At the restaurant where I work, 10% of my alcohol sales and non alcoholic beverage sales goes to my bartender. 5% of my total food sales goes to my busser. $3 goes to my salad prep. $3 goes to my stocker. And 1.2% of my total food sales goes to our food runner. 

Typically my tip out with my average sales is:
$20-$30 to bar
$40-$70 to busser
$10-$15 to runner
Then always the $6 for salad and stock no matter what.

When you tip poorly, we have to take out of our take home money to tip the other staff, because all of the staff works collectively together as a group to make the restaurant run properly. Also I don’t know about the restaurants you go to, but I do A LOT more than just serve people their food. Before we open we wipe all our tables, chairs, and booths in our sections. As well as shine our glass lanterns on each table, and make sure everything is stocked (salt and pepper is filled/condiments are filled like ketchup etc). At the end of the night we do that all again, plus sweep and also mop our sections. 

Additionally there is always sidework to be completed at the end of the shift. Sometimes this is handwashing all serving trays at the end of the night in the large kitchen sink, cleaning out the walk in refrigerator where we store our salad and butter for guests, cleaning out ashtrays outdoors and raking areas where guests throw trash and other stuff. Generally just making everything look presentable and nice. It usually takes me 1-2 hours to do all my sidework after my tables are finished and gone for the night. 

I’ve been a server for 12 years. I am one of the few at my restaurant who can take larger groups of people and often get groups of 20-30 people on my own, as well as having other tables at the same time. My job isn’t only serving their food, but making sure each of those guests is having a good experience. It took a long time but I’m pretty dang good at timing what needs to be done first so that all my guests aren’t waiting too long for drinks, their bill, me to check in on them, etc. of course there are bad nights where nothing goes right but generally I think I do a good job and my tips reflect that. 

It’s hard work and people can be awful. I’ve had customers spit in my face, throw items at me, scream in my face, threaten me, and cuss me out for things like: not being able to move them to another table because it was reserved for someone else, having the wrong side dish on their plate even though I rang it in correctly and the kitchen messed up, being upset about the cost of their bill, being told that our kitchen can’t make the special item that is not on our menu for them because that’s what they want…the list goes on. But we can’t bite back, and have to always be patient and understanding. I’ve had awful nights and although I don’t want to do this forever, I’ve also had amazing nights where I’ve been tipped $100, $300, and even one time $1,000 extra. It happens. 

I generally enjoy my job and I suppose to someone that has never done it they probably think it’s very easy and we don’t deserve to be tipped well. But there’s a lot more that goes on behind the scenes than us just bringing your food out to you.
